questions.text: Which of these is the general form of a grep command?
questions.explanation: Options first, then what to look for, then where to look. The pattern always comes before the filename — swapping them makes grep search a file named after your pattern.

questions.text: In the command grep 'mellon' myfile.txt, what does myfile.txt specify?
options: The pattern grep will look for
A file grep will write its output into
An option that changes how grep behaves
questions.explanation: 'mellon' is the pattern and myfile.txt is the file to search, so this prints every line of myfile.txt containing the string mellon. Neither is an option — options are the parts that start with a dash.

questions.text: grep can search a stream of text piped in from another command, with no filename given at all.
questions.explanation: That is what the cheat sheet means by searching standard output: ps -e | grep ssh hands grep the output of the first command instead of a file. Give it a filename and it reads the file; give it none and it reads whatever arrives on standard input.

questions.text: Fill in the command that prints the lines of myfile.txt containing the string mellon.
questions.explanation: The quotes around the pattern are not always required, but they stop the shell from touching characters like * and $ before grep ever sees them, so they are a good habit.

questions.text: A wildcard can stand in for the filename, as in grep -l 'robot' /var/log/*.
questions.explanation: The shell expands /var/log/* into the list of files before grep runs, so grep simply receives many filenames. That is also why it is worth quoting the pattern but not the filename — you usually want the shell to expand the filename.

questions.text: Match each grep option to what it does.
allChoices: Ignores case, so the pattern matches whatever the capitalisation
Matches whole words only, not pieces of longer words
Returns all the lines which do NOT match the pattern
Prints how many lines matched, instead of printing the lines
Prints the names of the files that contain a match
Shows the line number of each match
Shows only the matching part, not the whole line
Searches a directory and all of its subdirectories

pairs.match: Ignores case, so the pattern matches whatever the capitalisation
Matches whole words only, not pieces of longer words
Returns all the lines which do NOT match the pattern
Prints how many lines matched, instead of printing the lines
Prints the names of the files that contain a match
Shows the line number of each match
Shows only the matching part, not the whole line
Searches a directory and all of its subdirectories

questions.explanation: These eight cover most of what you will ever type. They combine freely: grep -in error app.log is case-insensitive and numbered.

questions.text: Match each of grep's context options to what it displays around a match.
allChoices: Displays 3 lines after each matching line
Displays 4 lines before each matching line
Displays 5 lines both before and after each matching line

pairs.match: Displays 3 lines after each matching line
Displays 4 lines before each matching line
Displays 5 lines both before and after each matching line

questions.explanation: A for after, B for before, C for context on both sides. These are what make grep usable on a stack trace, where the line that matches Exception is rarely the line you need to read.

questions.text: What does grep -i ^DA demo.txt return?
questions.context:
$ grep -i ^DA demo.txt
Dave works here
DANIEL is loud
options: Lines starting with da, in any mix of upper and lower case
Lines starting with the capitals DA only
Lines containing da anywhere in them
questions.explanation: Two things are happening: ^ anchors the match to the start of the line, and -i drops case sensitivity. So it matches a line beginning Dave and one beginning DANIEL alike. Without -i, only DANIEL comes back.

questions.text: Given the file below, grep -w "of" demo.txt returns both lines.
questions.context:
the sound of the sea
soften the blow
questions.explanation: Only the first line comes back. -w requires the match to be a whole word, and the of inside soften is part of a longer word. Drop -w and both lines match.

questions.text: What does grep -C 5 'Exception' error.log show?
options: Each matching line plus the 5 lines before and the 5 lines after it
Each matching line plus the 5 lines after it
Each matching line plus the 5 lines before it
questions.explanation: -C is both sides at once — it is the same as writing -A 5 -B 5. Use -A or -B when you only care about one direction.

questions.text: Fill in the option that makes grep search a directory and everything in its subdirectories. Include the dash.
questions.explanation: grep -r 'quickref.me' /var/log/nginx/ walks the whole tree under that directory. Without it, grep will not descend into a directory at all. Add -l to get just the filenames back: grep -rl.

questions.text: Fill in the option that returns every line which does NOT match the pattern. Include the dash.
questions.explanation: grep -v 'warning' /var/log/syslog gives you the log with the warnings taken out. It is the fastest way to strip noise you already know you can ignore.

questions.text: Fill in the option that puts the line number in front of each match. Include the dash.
questions.explanation: grep -n "go" demo.txt prints matches as 12:line text here, so you can jump straight to that line in an editor.

questions.text: The file app.log is shown below. What does grep -c error app.log print?
questions.context:
error: disk full, error again
all clear
questions.explanation: It prints 1, not 2. -c counts matching lines, and although the first line contains the word error twice, it is still one line. If you want to count occurrences rather than lines, run grep -o error app.log | wc -l — that gives 2. Cheat sheets often word this as 'count the number of matches', which is why it catches people out.

questions.text: What does -o change about grep's output?
options: It prints only the part of the line that matched, one match per line
It prints only the first match found in the whole file
It writes the output to a file instead of the screen
It prints only the lines that match exactly, start to finish
questions.explanation: Normally grep prints the entire line that contained a match. -o prints just the matched text — and if a line matched twice, you get two lines of output. That is what makes grep -o pattern file | wc -l a real count of occurrences.

questions.text: What does grep -l 'robot' /var/log/* give you?
options: The names of the files that contain a match, without the matching lines
The matching lines, each prefixed with its filename
The number of files that contain a match
The last line of every file that matches
questions.explanation: -l answers 'which files is this in?' rather than 'where exactly is it?'. It also stops reading each file at the first hit, which makes it quick across a big tree.

questions.text: Which two of these options stop grep from printing the matched text at all? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: -c prints a count and -l prints filenames; neither shows you the text that matched. -i, -n and -w all change which lines come back or how they are labelled, but you still get the lines themselves.

questions.text: grep -r 'TODO' src/ will find a match in src/utils/helpers.js.
questions.explanation: -r is recursive, so it descends through every subdirectory under src/. Without it, grep would refuse to read the directory at all.

questions.text: Drag each position anchor onto what it matches.
allChoices: The beginning of a line
The end of a line
An empty line: a beginning with an end and nothing between
The start of a word
The end of a word

pairs.match: The beginning of a line
The end of a line
An empty line: a beginning with an end and nothing between
The start of a word
The end of a word

questions.explanation: Anchors match a position rather than a character, which is why ^$ works: it is a start immediately followed by an end, so it only fits a line with nothing on it.

questions.text: Match each regex wildcard to what it means.
allChoices: Any single character
Optional, and can only occur once
Optional, and can occur more than once
Required, and can occur more than once

pairs.match: Any single character
Optional, and can only occur once
Optional, and can occur more than once
Required, and can occur more than once

questions.explanation: The pairing to hold on to is * against +: star allows zero, plus demands at least one. Note that ? and + need grep -E — plain grep treats them as ordinary characters.

questions.text: Match each quantifier to how many times it lets the previous item appear.
allChoices: Exactly n times
n times or more, with no upper limit
m times at most
Between n and m times

pairs.match: Exactly n times
n times or more, with no upper limit
m times at most
Between n and m times

questions.explanation: The comma is the whole trick: it is the side the comma is on that opens up. a{2} matches only aa, while a{2,} matches aa, aaa, aaaa and so on.

questions.text: Match each POSIX character class to what it matches.
allChoices: Any lower or upper case letter
Any number
Any lower or upper case letter, or a digit
Any whitespace

pairs.match: Any lower or upper case letter
Any number
Any lower or upper case letter, or a digit
Any whitespace

questions.explanation: These read better than a range does once a pattern gets long, and they are the portable way to say it. Remember they go inside a bracket expression to be used.

questions.text: Match each bracket range to what it matches.
allChoices: Any letter, written as two ranges
Any digit, written as one range
Any digit or letter, written as three ranges

pairs.match: Any letter, written as two ranges
Any digit, written as one range
Any digit or letter, written as three ranges

questions.explanation: A bracket expression matches exactly one character out of the set inside it. Ranges can be stacked without any separator, which is why [0-9A-Za-z] is three ranges in one bracket, not a list of three things.

questions.text: What does . match in a grep pattern?
options: Exactly one character, whatever it is
Any number of characters, including none
questions.explanation: It is exactly one of anything. That is why d..m matches dnsm inside dnsmasq: a d, two characters of any kind, then an m. To match a real full stop, escape it as \..

questions.text: The file below is searched with grep 'new*' words.txt. Which lines come back?
options: All three, because the w is optional
Only new and neww, because there must be at least one w
Only new, because it is an exact match
questions.explanation: * means zero or more of the character right before it, so new* is really 'ne, then any number of w including none'. That makes bare ne a match too. This is the single most common misreading of * — it is not the shell's match-anything wildcard.

questions.text: To use a POSIX class such as [:digit:] in a pattern, you have to put it inside another pair of brackets, like [[:digit:]].
questions.explanation: The class name is written [:digit:], but it is only meaningful inside a bracket expression, so the usable pattern is [[:digit:]]. Typing the bare form is an error — GNU grep answers with 'character class syntax is [[:space:]], not [:space:]'.

questions.text: Which option lets you write +, ? and (jason|jackson) without backslashes in front of them?
questions.explanation: -E turns on extended regular expressions. Without it grep uses basic ones, where + and ? are just ordinary characters and grouping has to be written \(...\). -e is a different thing entirely: it marks what follows as the pattern, which is how you search for something starting with a dash.

questions.text: What does grep -E 'ja(s|cks)on' filename match?
options: Lines containing ja, s, cks or on anywhere
Lines starting with ja and ending with on
questions.explanation: The brackets group the alternatives and | means or, so the pattern reads 'ja, then either s or cks, then on'. It needs -E — in basic grep those brackets would be literal characters.

questions.text: Fill in the pattern that returns only the lines starting with al.
questions.explanation: ^ pins the match to the start of the line, so alpha matches but normal does not. Without the anchor you would get both.

questions.text: Fill in the pattern that matches the empty lines in a file.
questions.explanation: Start of line immediately followed by end of line, with no room for a character in between. grep -c '^$' file is a quick way to count the blank lines, and grep -v '^$' file strips them out.
